blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Visual place recognition (VPR) localises a camera by retrieving similar geo-tagged images, and current foundation-model VPR models are accurate across cities, seasons and illumination, but not robust to adversarial perturbations: under a white-box attack on the ranking at an imperceptible budget of 1/255, SuperVLAD and BoQ keep at most 0.2% top-1 recall (R@1) on four benchmarks. We propose anchored rank-adversarial fine-tuning (ARAFT), which fine-tunes a released model with a listwise rank loss on each adversarial query's hardest positive and an anchor to the clean descriptor of the frozen pretrained model. Checkpoints are selected under a clean-accuracy budget fixed in advance, and the full trade-off is reported. Within five validation R@1 points of clean cost, plain adversarial training has no admissible checkpoint, whereas ARAFT raises robust R@1 from zero to 47.3 on SuperVLAD and 55.3 on BoQ; plain adversarial training exceeds this only at about three times the clean cost. Against unbudgeted plain adversarial training on the test sets, ARAFT matches its robust R@1 at 2/255 with about ten more clean R@1 points. At 4/255, plain adversarial training is 6-9 robust R@1 points ahead, while ARAFT still keeps its ten-point clean advantage. Developed on SuperVLAD, ARAFT transfers to BoQ without re-tuning, and its robustness holds against stronger optimisers, with no sign of gradient masking.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Visual place recognition (VPR) estimates where an image was taken by retrieving the most
similar images from a database of geo-tagged references. It provides the coarse
localisation and loop-closure candidates on which mobile robots, autonomous vehicles and
augmented-reality systems build their metric pose estimates. Modern VPR models encode each
image into a global descriptor with a pretrained backbone and a learned aggregation layer,
and rank the database by descriptor distance Arandjelović
et al. (2016) ; Berton et al. (2022) .
The most accurate current models build on the self-supervised DINOv2
backbone Oquab et al. (2024) with aggregators such as SALAD Izquierdo and
Civera (2024) ,
BoQ Ali-bey et al. (2024) and SuperVLAD Lu et al. (2024) , are trained on large
street-view collections Ali-bey et al. (2022) , and are deployed as released
checkpoints.

blocks.en:
We propose anchored rank-adversarial fine-tuning (ARAFT), which fine-tunes a
pretrained VPR model end to end on three terms: its original metric-learning loss on clean
images; a listwise rank loss that requires an adversarially perturbed query to rank its hardest positive above the nearest negatives; and an anchor that keeps the
perturbed query’s descriptor close to the clean descriptor of the frozen pretrained model.
Because adversarial fine-tuning trades clean accuracy for robustness and the trade-off
moves during training, we select checkpoints under an explicit clean-accuracy budget, fixed
before the experiments, and report the full trade-off curve rather than a single operating
point.

blocks.en:
We develop ARAFT on SuperVLAD and apply it unchanged to BoQ, and compare it with plain
adversarial training that uses the same attack, positives and schedule but no anchor.
Within a 5-point clean budget on the validation set, plain adversarial training has no
usable checkpoint on either model, whereas ARAFT reaches a robust R@1 of 47.3 (SuperVLAD)
and 55.3 (BoQ). Plain adversarial training exceeds this robustness only after giving up
about three times as much clean accuracy. On the test sets, ARAFT matches plain
adversarial training at its most robust checkpoint at 2 / 255 2/255 while keeping about ten more
clean R@1 points, and it is less robust at 4 / 255 4/255 and beyond. Its robustness holds against
stronger optimisers, with no sign of gradient masking. The clean cost under strong distribution shift, up to 24 points
on SPED and Nordland, remains the main limitation.

blocks.en:
Our contributions are: • a threat model and evaluation protocol for adversarial robustness of VPR, with
rank attacks, robustness curves and gradient-masking checks, and the finding that current foundation-model
VPR models have no robustness under it; • ARAFT, a rank-aware, anchored adversarial fine-tuning method for pretrained VPR
models, with checkpoint selection under an explicit clean-accuracy budget; • an evaluation on two architectures and four benchmarks, with paired significance
tests and ablations, showing that ARAFT is the only one of the compared methods that
provides robustness within a small clean budget, that it transfers to a second
architecture without re-tuning, and that protecting the hardest positive and anchoring
to the pretrained model are what make it work.

blocks.en: 2 Related work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
VPR is commonly cast as image retrieval with global
descriptors. NetVLAD Arandjelović
et al. (2016) made the VLAD aggregation of local CNN
features trainable end to end, and later work improved training data and
objectives Ali-bey et al. (2022) ; Berton et al. (2023) and aggregation, for example
with the feature-mixing MixVPR Ali-bey et al. (2023) . Recent state-of-the-art models
replace the CNN backbone with DINOv2 Oquab et al. (2024) : SALAD Izquierdo and
Civera (2024) aggregates its patch features by optimal transport, BoQ Ali-bey et al. (2024) with a bag of
learnable queries, and SuperVLAD Lu et al. (2024) with a compact VLAD layer and a
cross-image encoder. These models are typically trained on GSV-Cities with a
multi-similarity loss Wang et al. (2019) and evaluated on benchmarks that span
urban, seasonal and day–night change Berton et al. (2022) . Their robustness is
studied with respect to such natural changes, not to adversarial perturbations.

Defenses for ranking
models adapt adversarial training Madry et al. (2018) to triplet or ranking
losses. Zhou et al. Zhou et al. (2020) ; Zhou et al. (2024) proposed embedding-shifting and
anti-collapse objectives; hardness manipulation Zhou and Patel (2022) perturbs
training triplets to a chosen hardness, which makes adversarial training efficient; and
CA-TRIDE Tian et al. (2024) decouples the perturbation of anchors and candidates and
adapts it to the model’s state of collapse. These methods train ResNet-18 or smaller
networks on fine-grained retrieval benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CUB, Cars, SOP), the
later ones from ImageNet initialisation at budgets of 8 / 255 8/255 , and lose about 15–26 points
of clean R@1 on CUB and SOP. They do not start from a strong pretrained retrieval
model, do not consider geographic retrieval under distribution shift, and do not bound
the clean cost. Our plain adversarial-training baseline follows this line with a hinge
ranking loss, and our collapse guard is motivated by the collapse these works report.

blocks.en: 4.1 Models

blocks.en:

blocks.en:
SuperVLAD Lu et al. (2024) aggregates DINOv2
ViT-B/14 Oquab et al. (2024) patch features with a VLAD-style layer of four clusters
and one ghost cluster, followed by a cross-image encoder. We start from the released
checkpoint trained on GSV-Cities and use 322 × 322 322\times 322 inputs for training and testing.
The cross-image encoder attends across all images of a batch, so a descriptor depends on
the other images it is encoded with. An attack evaluated in batches would then succeed or
fail per batch rather than per query. In all attacks, validation and testing we therefore
encode every query and database image on its own, passing a sequence of length one to
the cross-image encoder. During training the clean loss keeps the original batch-level
encoding, and adversarial queries and anchor descriptors are encoded individually.
The positive and negative descriptors that serve as training targets are taken,
without gradients, from a batch-level pass over all 80 images of the batch; only the

blocks.en: 6 Discussion and limitations
blocks.zh: 6. 讨论和限制

blocks.en:
The two methods differ
most in the first adversarial epochs: after three epochs, plain adversarial training has
lost 7–10 clean points and ARAFT 1–2 (Fig. 1 ). A rank
loss only asks the attacked query to stay closer to its positive than to its negatives;
any rearrangement of the descriptor space that achieves this is acceptable to it,
including one that degrades the clean neighbourhoods learned during pretraining. The
anchor removes most of this freedom. By asking the attacked descriptor to coincide with the
pretrained model’s clean descriptor, it makes robustness and preservation of the pretrained
geometry the same goal. The ablations agree: without the anchor no checkpoint stays within
the budget, and with it the most robust checkpoint lies inside the budget, or for one
seed 0.4 points outside it, on both architectures. The rank target matters as well:
protecting the hardest positive instead of the closest one improves test robustness on
all four datasets.

The 5-point budget is enforced on
MSLS-val, and it does not transfer to strongly shifted domains: on SPED and Nordland ARAFT
loses 17–24 clean points. Part of this cost is due to fine-tuning on GSV-Cities at all,
since the clean twin alone loses up to 6.5 points, but most of it comes with robustness.
Because the anchor needs no labels, one possible remedy is to apply it to unlabelled
images of the target domain during fine-tuning. Until such a remedy is shown to work,
practitioners should measure the clean cost on data from their own deployment domain
rather than rely on the validation budget.

blocks.en:
Our robustness is empirical. We tested it with several
optimisers and budgets and found no sign of gradient masking, but we did not run
gradient-free or transfer attacks against the ARAFT models, and certified guarantees are
out of scope. Our rank-APGD uses APGD’s step-size control without its momentum term;
increasing its steps five-fold or adding restarts did not change the results. The
gradient-masking checks, the clean twin and the second seed are available for SuperVLAD only; BoQ was
trained and evaluated with one seed and the two headline attacks. The threat model covers
digital perturbations of the query; attacks on the database and physical or patch attacks
are not addressed. Finally, robustness at 4 / 255 4/255 on Nordland is near zero for every
method we trained, so on this benchmark only the 2 / 255 2/255 results indicate a meaningful
defense.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
Current foundation-model VPR models lose essentially all top-1 recall under
imperceptible white-box perturbations of the query. We introduced ARAFT, which fine-tunes a released VPR model with a
listwise rank loss on the hardest positive and an anchor to the frozen pretrained model,
and selects checkpoints under an explicit clean-accuracy budget. Both components matter:
the anchor makes robustness and preservation of the pretrained geometry the same goal,
and without it no checkpoint stays within the budget, while protecting the hardest
rather than the closest positive improves test robustness on all four datasets. Within a 5-point
validation budget, ARAFT raises the validation robust R@1 from zero to 47.3 on
SuperVLAD and 55.3 on BoQ, where plain adversarial training has no admissible checkpoint; it carries over to a second
architecture without re-tuning, and its robustness holds against stronger optimisers.
Plain adversarial training exceeds this robustness only at about three times the clean
cost. On the test sets, ARAFT matches plain adversarial training at its most robust
checkpoint at 2 / 255 2/255 with about ten more clean R@1 points, but falls 6–9 points behind
at 4 / 255 4/255 . Reducing the clean cost under strong
distribution shift, and extending robustness beyond the training budget, are the main
open problems for robust place recognition.
